hints: Focus on what each reagent does to the functional group, starting with HCN addition to the aldehyde.
Work out product Q first, the hydrolysis of the nitrile in P gives 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH.
Use the given stoichiometry, 2 x formula of Q minus 2 x H2O, to get the molecular formula of R, then simplify to the simplest ratio.
walkthrough:
**Find product P from cyanohydrin formation**

Aldehydes add HCN across the C=O bond to form a hydroxynitrile. Think of H adding to O and CN adding to C.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$$
So P is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$, formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{NO}$.

**Find product Q by acid hydrolysis**

Hot aqueous acid hydrolyses the nitrile group, $\text{-CN}$, to a carboxylic acid group, $\text{-COOH}$. The rest of the molecule is unchanged.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH} + \text{NH}_3$$
So Q is lactic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$, formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$. It has both an alcohol and a carboxylic acid group.

**Condense two Q to make R**

With a few drops of conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, the OH of one Q reacts with the COOH of the other to form esters. Two molecules combine and lose two waters to give a cyclic diester with no free OH or COOH left, which explains why R does not react with sodium.

$$2 \times \text{Q} \rightarrow \text{R} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$2(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3) - 2(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 - \text{H}_4\text{O}_2 = \text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$$

**Simplify to the empirical formula**

Empirical means the simplest whole number ratio. Divide the molecular formula by 2.

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_4 \div 2 = \text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$$

options.A: CHO is too simple and does not fit the atom count. Dividing C3H4O2 further is not possible with whole numbers, so this over-simplifies the correct ratio.
options.B: This is correct. 2 x C3H6O3 minus 2 x H2O gives molecular C6H8O4, which simplifies to empirical C3H4O2. This fits a diester with no remaining OH or COOH groups.
options.C: C3H5O2 has one hydrogen too many. It comes from not fully subtracting the 4 H atoms lost as 2 H2O during the double esterification.
options.D: C6H10O5 is wrong because it corresponds to losing only one water molecule from two Q molecules. The question states two waters are lost, and this option is also molecular, not empirical.
